items.stem: Along a geotechnical seismic array, horizontally polarized surface waves in bedrock of amplitude 0.045 m, wavelength 0.6 m, and frequency 40 Hz pass markers P at x₁ = 0.15 m and Q at x₂ = 0.51 m. What is the phase difference (in degrees) between P and Q?
items.workedSolution: Separation Δx = 0.51 m − 0.15 m = 0.36 m. Cycle span = 0.6 m, giving 0.600 cycles. Phase difference Δφ = 360° × 0.600 = 216°.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 360° to get 216° (C).

options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in radians without converting to degrees.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

items.stem: Figure depicts an electric-bass nickel-wound string anchored between bridge and headstock nut of fixed length 0.6 m oscillating in harmonic n = 4. Given a transverse wave speed of 144 m s⁻¹, calculate the frequency of this stationary wave.
items.workedSolution: For a string fixed at both ends in harmonic n = 4, λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.6) / 4 = 0.300 m. Thus f_n = v / λ_n = 144 / 0.300 = 480 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f_n = nv / (2L) to obtain 480 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the first-harmonic fundamental frequency v / (2L) instead of multiplying by harmonic number n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed-one-end pipe formula nv / (4L) instead of fixed-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing f = nv / L.

items.stem: Figure shows a cello A-string held taut between the fingerboard nut and tailpiece bridge of length 1.44 m vibrating in stationary harmonic mode n = 6 (wave speed 72 m s⁻¹). Determine the separation between consecutive nodes along the string.

markScheme.criterion: Uses d_NN = λ / 2 = L / n to obtain 0.240 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the node-to-adjacent-antinode distance λ / 4 instead of adjacent node spacing λ / 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides string length L by the total number of nodes (n + 1) instead of the number of loops n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates a full wavelength λ = 2L / n instead of the half-wavelength node-to-node spacing λ / 2.

options.label: D

items.workedSolution: Converting to SI units: λ = 5.14 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ m. Fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) = (5.14 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.8) / 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.06 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 2.06 × 10⁻³ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit separation and divides by screen distance (λd / D) instead of λD / d.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the distance from the central bright fringe to the first dark minimum (½ λD / d) instead of bright fringe spacing.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes an erroneous factor of 2, confusing double-slit fringe spacing with single-slit central maximum width.

items.stem: Figure illustrates a cyan argon-ion laser beam passing through a pair of closely spaced parallel apertures illuminating slits with slit separation 0.3 mm at distance 2.1 m from a screen where the adjacent bright fringe spacing is 3.72 mm. Calculate the wavelength of the coherent beam.
items.workedSolution: Rearranging fringe spacing Δy = λD / d gives λ = Δy × d / D = (3.72 × 10⁻³ × 3.00 × 10⁻⁴) / 2.1 = 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges double-slit relation to obtain λ = 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ m (B).

items.stem: Figure depicts a cyan argon-ion laser beam passing through a pair of closely spaced parallel apertures of wavelength 488 nm incident on slits with slit separation 0.28 mm and screen distance 1.4 m. How far from the central maximum does the order n = 5 bright fringe appear?
items.workedSolution: Single fringe spacing = λD / d = 2.44 × 10⁻³ m. Distance from n = 0 to the n = 5 bright fringe is y_5 = 5 × λD / d = 0.0122 m.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies destructive half-integer factor (n − ½) instead of constructive integer order n.

options.distractorRationale: Fencepost error: multiplies fringe spacing by (n + 1) fringes instead of n intervals from n = 0.

items.workedSolution: Since y_n = nλD / d, slit separation d = nλD / y_n = (4 × 4.60 × 10⁻⁷ × 3) / 0.0158 = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m.

options.distractorRationale: Divides total span by (n + 1) instead of n fringe intervals between n = 0 and order n.

items.stem: Figure shows a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence having 400 lines mm⁻¹ illuminated normally by a laser of wavelength 589 nm. Calculate the diffraction angle (in degrees) of the n = 3 maximum.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (3 × 5.89 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.707, so θ = 45.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 45.0° (D).

items.stem: Figure shows a collimated beam striking a transmission diffraction grating mounted on thevernier table of a spectrometer (500 lines mm⁻¹) normally and producing its n = 2 principal maximum at an angle of 32.1°. Calculate the beam's wavelength.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm strikes a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence ruled with 300 lines mm⁻¹. At what angle θ from the normal is the order n = 3 principal maximum observed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (3 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁷) / 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.585, so θ = 35.8°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 35.8° (D).

items.stem: On a transmission diffraction grating mounted on thevernier table of a spectrometer with 500 lines mm⁻¹, the order n = 3 diffraction maximum of a monochromatic beam is measured at θ = 57.1° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength of the light?
items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(57.1°) / 3 = 5.60 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.60 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Figure shows an astronomical spectrograph test bench using a normal-incidence transmission grating having 300 lines mm⁻¹ illuminated normally by a laser of wavelength 514 nm. Calculate the diffraction angle (in degrees) of the n = 2 maximum.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (2 × 5.14 × 10⁻⁷) / 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.308, so θ = 18.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 18.0° (D).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 633 nm passes through a darkroom diffraction bench where coherent plane waves pass through a single narrow aperture of slit width 0.12 mm onto a screen 3.5 m away. What is the full linear width of the central bright diffraction maximum on the screen?
items.workedSolution: First diffraction minima lie at θ = ±λ / b, giving half-width y₁ = λD / b = 0.0185 m. Full central maximum width w = 2λD / b = 0.0369 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0369 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit width b and divides by screen distance D instead of 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates λD / b (the distance from the centre to one first-order minimum) instead of the full central maximum width 2λD / b.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 when doubling the first-minimum half-width.

items.stem: To calibrate a darkroom diffraction bench where coherent plane waves pass through a single narrow aperture using a laser of wavelength 514 nm and screen distance 3 m, an engineer measures the full central diffraction maximum width to be 25.7 mm. Calculate the aperture width b.
items.workedSolution: Since full central maximum width w = 2λD / b, rearranging gives b = 2λD / w = (2 × 5.14 × 10⁻⁷ × 3) / 0.0257 = 1.20 × 10⁻⁴ m.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges w = 2λD / b to obtain b = 1.20 × 10⁻⁴ m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies λ by w and divides by 2D instead of computing b = 2λD / w.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in w = 2λD / b (treating full central width as λD / b), underestimating slit width by half.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 4λD / w instead of 2λD / w.

items.workedSolution: Since full central maximum width w = 2λD / b, rearranging gives b = 2λD / w = (2 × 6.70 × 10⁻⁷ × 3.5) / 0.0261 = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ m.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges w = 2λD / b to obtain b = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ m (C).

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 4λD / w instead of 2λD / w.

items.stem: Emitting a continuous tone of frequency 750 Hz, a fire-appliance warning horn approaches directly towards a pedestrian waiting at a kerbside crossing at a constant speed of 88 m s⁻¹. Taking the speed of sound in still air as 340 m s⁻¹, what frequency is detected by the stationary observer?
items.workedSolution: For a source moving towards a stationary observer, f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (750 × 340) / (340 − 88) = 1.01e+3 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 1.01e+3 Hz (D).

items.stem: Sounding continuously at 440 Hz, an express electric locomotive horn recedes directly away from a commuter standing beside the straight track through still air (speed of sound 343 m s⁻¹). If the stationary observer records a shifted frequency of 350 Hz, what is the speed of the source?

markScheme.criterion: Solves f' = fv / (v ∓ v_s) for v_s = 88.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: In still air where sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹, a fixed beacon (an autonomous test-track vehicle ultrasonic-audible beacon) emits 920 Hz. As a second instrumented test vehicle on the straight lane travels directly away from the source, its microphone detects 736 Hz. Determine the observer's speed.
items.workedSolution: For a stationary source and moving observer, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v. Rearranging gives v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 340 × |736 / 920 − 1| = 68.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 68.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Figure depicts wavefronts of frequency 920 Hz radiated by a stationary emergency ambulance siren while a pursuit motorcycle carrying a calibrated microphone travels directly towards the source at 60 m s⁻¹ (sound speed 330 m s⁻¹). Calculate the observed frequency.
items.workedSolution: For a moving observer and stationary source, f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 920 × (330 + 60) / 330 = 1.09e+3 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 1.09e+3 Hz (C).

items.stem: A stationary aerobatic prop-plane acoustic beacon emits a steady 920 Hz note in still air (speed of sound 330 m s⁻¹). If a runway calibration vehicle travels directly away from the source at 72 m s⁻¹, what frequency does it detect?
items.workedSolution: For a moving observer and stationary source, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 920 × (330 − 72) / 330 = 719 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 719 Hz (A).

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(50°) = 34.7 W m⁻² (B).

items.stem: On a fibre-optics free-space polarization controller bench with an ideal linear analyzer, a plane-polarized beam of intensity 72 W m⁻² passes through an ideal linear analyzer, emerging with reduced intensity 42.3 W m⁻² (Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ). What acute angle θ is the analyzer's transmission axis rotated relative to the incident polarization?
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(42.3 / 72) = 0.766, giving θ = arccos(0.766) = 40.0°.

items.stem: On a liquid-crystal display (LCD) backlight test rig using thin-film linear polaroid sheets, a vertically plane-polarized beam of intensity 96 W m⁻² is incident normally on an ideal linear analyzer whose transmission axis is rotated by 20° from the vertical. What is the transmitted intensity?
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 96 × cos²(20°) = 96 × 0.883 = 84.8 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(20°) = 84.8 W m⁻² (C).

items.stem: On a microwave horn link employing parallel wire-grid polarizing frames, a vertically plane-polarized beam of intensity 240 W m⁻² is incident normally on an ideal linear analyzer whose transmission axis is rotated by 40° from the vertical. What is the transmitted intensity?
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 240 × cos²(40°) = 240 × 0.587 = 141 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(40°) = 141 W m⁻² (C).

items.stem: To attenuate a plane-polarized beam from 32 W m⁻² down to 13.2 W m⁻² on a spectrophotometer polarization module with a precision rotary Vernier analyzer, an ideal analyzer is rotated through an acute angle θ from alignment (I = I₀ cos²θ). Determine θ.
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(13.2 / 32) = 0.643, giving θ = arccos(0.643) = 50.0°.

items.stem: During a calibration on a fibre-optics free-space polarization controller bench with an ideal linear analyzer, plane-polarized radiation of intensity 240 W m⁻² strikes an analyzer tilted at θ = 35° relative to the incident polarization axis. Determine the transmitted intensity.
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 240 × cos²(35°) = 240 × 0.671 = 161 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(35°) = 161 W m⁻² (C).

items.stem: On a stress-photoelasticity polariscope bench with graduated rotary analyzer mount, a plane-polarized beam of intensity 160 W m⁻² passes through an ideal linear analyzer, emerging with reduced intensity 40.0 W m⁻² (Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ). What acute angle θ is the analyzer's transmission axis rotated relative to the incident polarization?
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(40.0 / 160) = 0.500, giving θ = arccos(0.500) = 60.0°.

items.stem: On an optical-mineralogy bench testing transmission through crossed and angled polaroids, a plane-polarized beam of intensity 120 W m⁻² passes through an ideal linear analyzer, emerging with reduced intensity 70.4 W m⁻² (Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ). What acute angle θ is the analyzer's transmission axis rotated relative to the incident polarization?
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(70.4 / 120) = 0.766, giving θ = arccos(0.766) = 40.0°.

items.stem: Figure shows plane-polarized light of intensity 24 W m⁻² entering an ideal analyzer set at an angle of 20° to the incident electric-field plane on a stress-photoelasticity polariscope bench with graduated rotary analyzer mount. Calculate the emerging beam intensity.
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 24 × cos²(20°) = 24 × 0.883 = 21.2 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(20°) = 21.2 W m⁻² (C).

items.stem: Along a dielectric waveguide bench, guided millimetre-wave oscillations of amplitude 0.055 m, wavelength 0.24 m, and frequency 4 Hz pass markers P at x₁ = 0.036 m and Q at x₂ = 0.216 m. What is the phase difference (in degrees) between P and Q?
items.workedSolution: Separation Δx = 0.216 m − 0.036 m = 0.18 m. Cycle span = 0.24 m, giving 0.750 cycles. Phase difference Δφ = 360° × 0.750 = 270°.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates fractional cycle separation and multiplies by 360° to get 270° (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes phase difference in radians without converting to degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses half a cycle (180°) instead of a full cycle (360°) in the phase-difference formula.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the fractional cycle ratio (dividing cycle span by separation instead of separation by cycle span).

items.stem: A single probe in an ultrasonic non-destructive testing bench records the displacement–time trace y(t) of elastic shear waves in a polymer bar with amplitude 0.018 m and period 0.25 s. If the wave travels through the medium at 0.96 m s⁻¹, what is its wavelength?
items.workedSolution: From the displacement–time trace, the period is T = 0.25 s. Using λ = vT with v = 0.96 m s⁻¹ gives λ = 0.96 × 0.25 = 0.240 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = vT = 0.96 m s⁻¹ × 0.25 s to obtain 0.240 m (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides period by wave speed (T / v) instead of multiplying vT.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reads the full two-cycle time span 2T as a single period when computing λ = vT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides wave speed by period (v / T), treating period T on the time axis as if it were frequency f.

items.stem: Figure illustrates a sonometer constantan wire clamped rigidly between two knife-edge bridges of length 0.72 m resonating in harmonic mode n = 4 when driven at 466.7 Hz. Calculate the transverse wave speed on the string.
items.workedSolution: For harmonic n = 4 on a string of length L = 0.72 m fixed at both ends, λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.72) / 4 = 0.360 m. Wave speed v = f_n λ_n = 466.6666666666667 × 0.360 = 168 m s⁻¹.

items.workedSolution: Since y_n = nλD / d, slit separation d = nλD / y_n = (4 × 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.4) / 0.0131 = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th bright fringe displacement as a single fringe spacing, omitting the factor of n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies dark-fringe factor (n − ½) instead of integer n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides total span by (n + 1) instead of n fringe intervals between n = 0 and order n.

items.stem: Coherent light of wavelength 660 nm from a cyan argon-ion laser beam passing through a pair of closely spaced parallel apertures passes through slits of slit separation 0.28 mm onto a screen 1.75 m away. What is the linear distance on the screen from the central bright fringe (n = 0) to the n = 5 bright fringe?
items.workedSolution: Single fringe spacing = λD / d = 4.13 × 10⁻³ m. Distance from n = 0 to the n = 5 bright fringe is y_5 = 5 × λD / d = 0.0206 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates single adjacent fringe spacing λD / d instead of multiplying by order n.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies destructive half-integer factor (n − ½) instead of constructive integer order n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Fencepost error: multiplies fringe spacing by (n + 1) fringes instead of n intervals from n = 0.

What is the slit separation?
items.workedSolution: Since y_n = nλD / d, slit separation d = nλD / y_n = (4 × 4.88 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.75) / 0.0122 = 2.80 × 10⁻⁴ m.

items.stem: Figure depicts a collimated green DPSS diode-pumped laser directed normally onto two narrow parallel slits of wavelength 460 nm incident on slits with slit separation 0.55 mm and screen distance 2.5 m. How far from the central maximum does the order n = 3 bright fringe appear?
items.workedSolution: Single fringe spacing = λD / d = 2.09 × 10⁻³ m. Distance from n = 0 to the n = 3 bright fringe is y_3 = 3 × λD / d = 6.27 × 10⁻³ m.

items.stem: On an optical bench, a collimated green DPSS diode-pumped laser directed normally onto two narrow parallel slits (wavelength 488 nm) illuminates a double slit of slit separation 0.55 mm. Calculate the displacement from the central maximum to the 3th-order bright maximum on a screen 3 m behind the slits.
items.workedSolution: Single fringe spacing = λD / d = 2.66 × 10⁻³ m. Distance from n = 0 to the n = 3 bright fringe is y_3 = 3 × λD / d = 7.99 × 10⁻³ m.

items.stem: Figure shows a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence having 250 lines mm⁻¹ illuminated normally by a laser of wavelength 650 nm. Calculate the diffraction angle (in degrees) of the n = 2 maximum.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 250 = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (2 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁷) / 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.325, so θ = 19.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 19.0° (D).

items.stem: On an astronomical spectrograph test bench using a normal-incidence transmission grating with 400 lines mm⁻¹, the order n = 3 diffraction maximum of a monochromatic beam is measured at θ = 45.0° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength of the light?
items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(45.0°) / 3 = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 589 nm strikes a collimated laser wavelength-calibration rig fitted with a plane transmission grating ruled with 500 lines mm⁻¹. At what angle θ from the normal is the order n = 1 principal maximum observed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (1 × 5.89 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.294, so θ = 17.1°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 17.1° (C).

items.stem: Figure shows a collimated beam striking a telecommunications optical-spectrum test stage with a precision ruled grating (500 lines mm⁻¹) normally and producing its n = 3 principal maximum at an angle of 40.2°. Calculate the beam's wavelength.
items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(40.2°) / 3 = 4.30 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 4.30 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 514 nm strikes a transmission diffraction grating mounted on thevernier table of a spectrometer ruled with 400 lines mm⁻¹. At what angle θ from the normal is the order n = 2 principal maximum observed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (2 × 5.14 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.411, so θ = 24.3°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 24.3° (D).

items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(14.9°) / 1 = 5.14 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (1 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.325, so θ = 19.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 19.0° (C).

items.stem: On an optics rail, a semiconductor-wafer metrology aperture illuminated squarely by a stabilised laser diode (width 0.22 mm) diffracts a beam of wavelength 450 nm onto a screen at distance 2.5 m. Determine the full width w of the central bright fringe.
items.workedSolution: First diffraction minima lie at θ = ±λ / b, giving half-width y₁ = λD / b = 5.11 × 10⁻³ m. Full central maximum width w = 2λD / b = 0.0102 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0102 m (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates λD / b (the distance from the centre to one first-order minimum) instead of the full central maximum width 2λD / b.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 when doubling the first-minimum half-width.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges w = 2λD / b to obtain b = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m (C).

items.stem: In still air where sound travels at 336 m s⁻¹, a high-speed sled mounted with an acoustic whistle sounds at 820 Hz while moving at 60 m s⁻¹ as it approaches directly towards a fixed microphone at the end of the test track. Which frequency is recorded?
items.workedSolution: For a source moving towards a stationary observer, f' = fv / (v − v_s) = (820 × 336) / (336 − 60) = 998 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 998 Hz (D).

items.stem: Sounding continuously at 560 Hz, an express electric locomotive horn recedes directly away from a commuter standing beside the straight track through still air (speed of sound 343 m s⁻¹). If the stationary observer records a shifted frequency of 467 Hz, what is the speed of the source?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging f' = fv / (v + v_s) gives v + v_s = vf / f' = (343 × 560) / 467, yielding v_s = 68.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves f' = fv / (v ∓ v_s) for v_s = 68.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Sounding continuously at 820 Hz, an express electric locomotive horn approaches directly towards a commuter standing beside the straight track through still air (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). items.stem: Figure depicts wavefronts of frequency 400 Hz radiated by a stationary aerobatic prop-plane acoustic beacon while a runway calibration vehicle travels directly away from the source at 68 m s⁻¹ (sound speed 340 m s⁻¹). Calculate the observed frequency.
items.workedSolution: For a moving observer and stationary source, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 400 × (340 − 68) / 340 = 320 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v − v_o) / v = 320 Hz (A).

items.stem: In a darkroom optics experiment, a violet semiconductor laser beam incident perpendicular to a dual-slit foil slide emits coherent light of wavelength 650 nm onto a double slit of slit separation 0.16 mm, with an observation screen positioned 3.6 m away.
items.workedSolution: (a) Fringe spacing = λD / d = (6.50 × 10⁻⁷ × 3.6) / 1.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.0146 m. (b) First dark fringe distance = ½ × 0.0146 = 7.31 × 10⁻³ m. (c) At order n = 2, path difference = nλ = 2 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.30 × 10⁻⁶ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units and substitutes into λD / (slit separation).

workingSteps: Constructive interference at order n requires path difference Δℓ = nλ.

items.stem: During a straight-line Doppler measurement in still air (sound speed 330 m s⁻¹), an aerobatic prop-plane acoustic beacon sounding at 520 Hz moves away from the observer at 36 m s⁻¹ while a runway calibration vehicle travels directly away from the source at 38 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ′ = (v + v_s) / f = 0.704 m. (b) v_rel = v − v_o = 292 m s⁻¹. (c) f′ = v_rel / λ′ = 415 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Computes shifted wavelength in air ahead of/behind moving source.
Combines wave speed v and observer speed v_o with correct relative sign.
Divides relative wave speed from (b) by wavelength from (a).

items.stem: Sound waves propagate at 343 m s⁻¹ through calm air while an emergency ambulance siren, emitting a steady 680 Hz signal, recedes directly away from a stationary roadside acoustic logger at speed 68 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Unshifted wavelength λ₀ = v / f = 0.504 m. (b) In the region towards the observer, λ′ = (v + v_s) / f = 0.604 m. (c) Observed frequency f′ = v / λ′ = 567 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f′ = v / λ′ or exact moving-source Doppler formula.

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 460 nm strikes a physics Required Practical bench where a laser beam hits a clamped transmission grating squarely ruled with 400 lines mm⁻¹. At what angle θ from the normal is the order n = 3 principal maximum observed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 400 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (3 × 4.60 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.552, so θ = 33.5°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 33.5° (D).

items.stem: On a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence with 500 lines mm⁻¹, the order n = 2 diffraction maximum of a monochromatic beam is measured at θ = 36.1° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength of the light?

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Figure shows a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence having 500 lines mm⁻¹ illuminated normally by a laser of wavelength 532 nm. Calculate the diffraction angle (in degrees) of the n = 2 maximum.
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (2 × 5.32 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.532, so θ = 32.1°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 32.1° (D).

items.stem: On an astronomical spectrograph test bench using a normal-incidence transmission grating with 300 lines mm⁻¹, the order n = 2 diffraction maximum of a monochromatic beam is measured at θ = 20.7° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength of the light?

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Figure shows a collimated beam striking a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence (300 lines mm⁻¹) normally and producing its n = 3 principal maximum at an angle of 32.0°. Calculate the beam's wavelength.
items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(32.0°) / 3 = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 633 nm strikes a collimated laser wavelength-calibration rig fitted with a plane transmission grating ruled with 500 lines mm⁻¹. At what angle θ from the normal is the order n = 2 principal maximum observed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 500 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (2 × 6.33 × 10⁻⁷) / 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.633, so θ = 39.3°.

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = 10⁻³ / N and solves d sin θ = nλ to get 39.3° (D).

items.stem: On a metrology optical encoder bench illuminating a ruled glass grating at zero angle of incidence with 200 lines mm⁻¹, the order n = 3 diffraction maximum of a monochromatic beam is measured at θ = 18.0° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength of the light?
items.workedSolution: Slit spacing d = 10⁻³ / 200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives λ = d sin(18.0°) / 3 = 5.14 × 10⁻⁷ m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes d = 10⁻³ / N and λ = d sin θ / n = 5.14 × 10⁻⁷ m (A).

items.stem: When a laser beam of wavelength 545 nm hits a darkroom laser diffractometer holding a multi-slit transmission grating perpendicular to the beam having 480 lines mm⁻¹ squarely, what is the largest integer order n for which a principal maximum is formed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 480 = 2.08 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 2.08 × 10⁻⁶ / 5.45 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.82. Taking the floor gives n_max = 3.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 3.82 and takes floor to get n_max = 3 (A).

items.stem: Figure depicts a discharge-lamp spectroscopy setup where collimated monochromatic light strikes a grating normally (450 lines mm⁻¹) illuminated squarely by coherent light of wavelength 575 nm. What total number of bright principal maxima can be detected on a semicircular detector track?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 450 = 2.22 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 3.86 and n_max = 3. Including ±1..±3 and n = 0 gives 2(3) + 1 = 7 principal maxima.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 4.80 and takes floor to get n_max = 4 (A).

items.stem: A laser beam of wavelength 655 nm is incident normally on a telecommunications optical-spectrum test stage with a precision ruled grating with 320 lines mm⁻¹. Including the central zero-order beam, how many total principal maxima emerge across the forward semicircle (−90° ≤ θ ≤ +90°)?
items.workedSolution: d = 10⁻³ / 320 = 3.13 × 10⁻⁶ m, so d / λ = 4.77 and n_max = 4. Including ±1..±4 and n = 0 gives 2(4) + 1 = 9 principal maxima.

items.stem: Collimated light of wavelength 640 nm strikes a telecommunications optical-spectrum test stage with a precision ruled grating ruled with 200 lines mm⁻¹ at normal incidence. What is the highest diffraction order n_max observable?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ / 6.40 × 10⁻⁷ = 7.81. Taking the floor gives n_max = 7.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 7.81 and takes floor to get n_max = 7 (A).

items.stem: When a laser beam of wavelength 480 nm hits a student goniometer spectrometer carrying a ruled glass diffraction grating having 550 lines mm⁻¹ squarely, what is the largest integer order n for which a principal maximum is formed?
items.workedSolution: Grating spacing d = 10⁻³ / 550 = 1.82 × 10⁻⁶ m. Since sin θ ≤ 1, n ≤ d / λ = 1.82 × 10⁻⁶ / 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.79. Taking the floor gives n_max = 3.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates d / λ = 3.79 and takes floor to get n_max = 3 (A).

items.stem: Figure shows a normal-incidence beam of wavelength 430 nm diffracted by an astronomical spectrograph test bench using a normal-incidence transmission grating having 300 lines mm⁻¹ onto a planar screen 1.6 m away; consider the n = 3 bright order.
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 10⁻³ / 300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) sin θ = nλ / d = 0.387, so θ = 22.8°. (c) On the flat screen, y = D tan θ = 1.6 × tan(22.8°) = 0.672 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises large-angle geometry y = D tan θ rather than small-angle D sin θ.

items.stem: Emitting a continuous tone of frequency 820 Hz, a fire-appliance warning horn approaches directly towards a pedestrian waiting at a kerbside crossing at a constant speed of 72 m s⁻¹. Taking the speed of sound in still air as 340 m s⁻¹, what frequency is detected by the stationary observer?

markScheme.criterion: Applies exact moving-source Doppler formula to obtain 1.04e+3 Hz (D).

items.stem: A stationary emergency ambulance siren radiates sound at 400 Hz in still air (speed of sound 343 m s⁻¹). Meanwhile, a pursuit motorcycle carrying a calibrated microphone travels directly away from the source and measures a frequency of 309 Hz. What is the speed of the moving observer?
items.workedSolution: For a stationary source and moving observer, f′ = f(v − v_o) / v. Rearranging gives v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 343 × |309 / 400 − 1| = 78.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 78.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Figure depicts wavefronts of frequency 780 Hz radiated by a stationary emergency ambulance siren while a pursuit motorcycle carrying a calibrated microphone travels directly towards the source at 72 m s⁻¹ (sound speed 343 m s⁻¹). Calculate the observed frequency.
items.workedSolution: For a moving observer and stationary source, f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 780 × (343 + 72) / 343 = 944 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f′ = f(v + v_o) / v = 944 Hz (C).

items.stem: A stationary racing telemetry drone emitting a steady acoustic tone emits a steady 640 Hz note in still air (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). If a camera car driving along the straightaway travels directly away from the source at 64 m s⁻¹, what frequency does it detect?

items.stem: A stationary racing telemetry drone emitting a steady acoustic tone radiates sound at 920 Hz in still air (speed of sound 330 m s⁻¹). Meanwhile, a camera car driving along the straightaway travels directly towards the source and measures a frequency of 1.08e+3 Hz. What is the speed of the moving observer?
items.workedSolution: For a stationary source and moving observer, f′ = f(v + v_o) / v. Rearranging gives v_o = v|f′ / f − 1| = 330 × |1.08e+3 / 920 − 1| = 56.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f′ = f(v ± v_o) / v to obtain v_o = 56.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.workedSolution: Converting to SI units: λ = 6.33 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ m. Fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) = (6.33 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.4) / 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.60 × 10⁻³ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses fringe spacing = λD / (slit separation) to obtain 7.60 × 10⁻³ m (C).

items.stem: Coherent light of wavelength 488 nm from a blue gallium-nitride laser module aligned along an optical rail toward two parallel slits strikes a double slit of slit separation 0.24 mm placed 2.2 m from a screen. items.workedSolution: The first single-slit minimum occurs at θ = λ / b while the n-th double-slit maximum is at θ = nλ / d. Coincidence at n = 3 gives b = d / 3 = 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ / 3 = 8.00 × 10⁻⁵ m.

markScheme.criterion: Equates λ / b = nλ / d to obtain b = d / 3 = 8.00 × 10⁻⁵ m (B).

items.stem: Using a collimated green DPSS diode-pumped laser directed normally onto two narrow parallel slits of wavelength 589 nm at screen distance 2.2 m, two parallel slits each of individual slit width 0.05 mm are separated by centre-to-centre slit separation 0.15 mm. items.workedSolution: Interference maxima satisfy sin θ = nλ / d and the first single-slit minimum satisfies sin θ = λ / b. Dividing gives n = d / b = 1.50 × 10⁻⁴ / 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 3.

items.stem: Light of wavelength 514 nm from a sodium vapour discharge lamp filtered and collimated onto a Young's double-slit plate illuminates a double slit of slit separation 0.24 mm in which each slit has finite width 0.06 mm. items.stem: On a glare-suppression laboratory rig directing a collimated beam onto linear polarizing films, a plane-polarized beam of intensity 144 W m⁻² passes through an ideal linear analyzer, emerging with reduced intensity 47.4 W m⁻² (Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ). What acute angle θ is the analyzer's transmission axis rotated relative to the incident polarization?
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(47.4 / 144) = 0.574, giving θ = arccos(0.574) = 55.0°.

items.stem: During a calibration on a fibre-optics free-space polarization controller bench with an ideal linear analyzer, plane-polarized radiation of intensity 144 W m⁻² strikes an analyzer tilted at θ = 70° relative to the incident polarization axis. Determine the transmitted intensity.
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 144 × cos²(70°) = 144 × 0.117 = 16.8 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(70°) = 16.8 W m⁻² (B).

items.stem: On a liquid-crystal display (LCD) backlight test rig using thin-film linear polaroid sheets, a plane-polarized beam of intensity 32 W m⁻² passes through an ideal linear analyzer, emerging with reduced intensity 10.5 W m⁻² (Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ). What acute angle θ is the analyzer's transmission axis rotated relative to the incident polarization?
items.workedSolution: From I = I₀ cos²θ, cos θ = √(10.5 / 32) = 0.574, giving θ = arccos(0.574) = 55.0°.

items.stem: On a spectrophotometer polarization module with a precision rotary Vernier analyzer, a vertically plane-polarized beam of intensity 72 W m⁻² is incident normally on an ideal linear analyzer whose transmission axis is rotated by 35° from the vertical. What is the transmitted intensity?
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 72 × cos²(35°) = 72 × 0.671 = 48.3 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(35°) = 48.3 W m⁻² (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Both omits the square root and uses arcsin(I / I₀).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes the complement angle 90° − θ (using arcsin √(I / I₀) instead of arccos √(I / I₀)).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to take the square root of I / I₀ before taking arccos, solving cos θ = I / I₀ instead of cos²θ = I / I₀.

items.stem: On a laser power-attenuation stage feeding a calibrated silicon photodiode detector, a vertically plane-polarized beam of intensity 120 W m⁻² is incident normally on an ideal linear analyzer whose transmission axis is rotated by 70° from the vertical. What is the transmitted intensity?
items.workedSolution: Because the incident beam is already plane-polarized, Malus's law gives I = I₀ cos²θ = 120 × cos²(70°) = 120 × 0.117 = 14.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = I₀ cos²(70°) = 14.0 W m⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Mistakenly applies the ½ unpolarized-light factor to a beam that is already plane-polarized.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses I₀ cos θ (electric-field amplitude projection) instead of Malus's intensity law I₀ cos²θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses I₀ sin²θ (measuring the complement angle to the extinction axis instead of the transmission axis).

items.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity 64 W m⁻² enters a fibre-optics free-space polarization controller bench with an ideal linear analyzer, passing first through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁ and then through an ideal analyzer A whose axis is rotated by 70° to P₁ (for plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, analyzer transmission is I = I₁ cos²θ). What intensity emerges from analyzer A?
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 32.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(70°) = ½(64) cos²(70°) = 3.74 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(70°) = 3.74 W m⁻² (A).

options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of ½ at polarizer P₁ for unpolarized incident light, computing I₀ cos²θ instead of ½ I₀ cos²θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the ½ factor at P₁ correctly but uses cos θ instead of cos²θ at analyzer A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses ½ I₀ sin²θ (complement angle) instead of ½ I₀ cos²θ.

items.stem: An unpolarized beam of unknown intensity I₀ passes sequentially through ideal polarizer P₁ and analyzer A (oriented at 65° to P₁) on a microwave horn link employing parallel wire-grid polarizing frames. If the final emerging intensity is 3.21 W m⁻² (where polarized transmission obeys I = I₁ cos²θ), what is the incident unpolarized intensity I₀?
items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(65°) = (2 × 3.21) / 0.179 = 36.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 36.0 W m⁻² (D).

options.distractorRationale: Multiplies I / cos²θ by ½ instead of 2 when inverting I₁ = ½ I₀.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides 2I by cos θ instead of cos²θ when inverting Malus's law.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the ½ intensity reduction at polarizer P₁, computing I / cos²θ instead of 2I / cos²θ.

items.stem: In a two-filter test on a liquid-crystal display (LCD) backlight test rig using thin-film linear polaroid sheets, an unpolarized beam of intensity 220 W m⁻² traverses ideal polarizer P₁ followed by analyzer A angled at 30° to P₁'s axis (I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light). Determine the emerging intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 110 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(30°) = ½(220) cos²(30°) = 82.5 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(30°) = 82.5 W m⁻² (B).

items.stem: On a microwave horn link employing parallel wire-grid polarizing frames, unpolarized light traverses ideal polarizer P₁ and analyzer A tilted at θ = 65° relative to P₁, yielding a transmitted intensity of 5.72 W m⁻² (I = I₁ cos²θ for plane-polarized light). items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(65°) = (2 × 5.72) / 0.179 = 64.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 64.0 W m⁻² (D).

items.stem: Figure shows unpolarized radiation of intensity 112 W m⁻² on an optical bench fitted with a Glan-Thompson calcite polarizer and a rotatable analyzer passing sequentially through polarizer P₁ and analyzer A inclined at θ = 70° relative to P₁ (Malus's law for polarized light: I = I₁ cos²θ). Calculate the final transmitted intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 56.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(70°) = ½(112) cos²(70°) = 6.55 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(70°) = 6.55 W m⁻² (A).

items.stem: Figure shows unpolarized radiation of intensity 112 W m⁻² on an optical-mineralogy bench testing transmission through crossed and angled polaroids passing sequentially through polarizer P₁ and analyzer A inclined at θ = 65° relative to P₁ (Malus's law for polarized light: I = I₁ cos²θ). Calculate the final transmitted intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 56.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(65°) = ½(112) cos²(65°) = 10.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(65°) = 10.0 W m⁻² (A).

items.stem: An unpolarized beam of unknown intensity I₀ passes sequentially through ideal polarizer P₁ and analyzer A (oriented at 35° to P₁) on a microwave horn link employing parallel wire-grid polarizing frames. If the final emerging intensity is 21.5 W m⁻² (where polarized transmission obeys I = I₁ cos²θ), what is the incident unpolarized intensity I₀?
items.workedSolution: Since I = ½ I₀ cos²θ, rearranging gives I₀ = 2I / cos²(35°) = (2 × 21.5) / 0.671 = 64.0 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Solves I = ½ I₀ cos²θ to obtain I₀ = 64.0 W m⁻² (D).

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(65°) = 3.21 W m⁻² (A).

items.stem: Figure shows unpolarized radiation of intensity 220 W m⁻² on an optical bench fitted with a Glan-Thompson calcite polarizer and a rotatable analyzer passing sequentially through polarizer P₁ and analyzer A inclined at θ = 25° relative to P₁ (Malus's law for polarized light: I = I₁ cos²θ). Calculate the final transmitted intensity.
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 110 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(25°) = ½(220) cos²(25°) = 90.4 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(25°) = 90.4 W m⁻² (B).

items.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity 128 W m⁻² enters a liquid-crystal display (LCD) backlight test rig using thin-film linear polaroid sheets, passing first through an ideal vertical polarizer P₁ and then through an ideal analyzer A whose axis is rotated by 25° to P₁ (for plane-polarized light of intensity I₁, analyzer transmission is I = I₁ cos²θ). What intensity emerges from analyzer A?
items.workedSolution: Ideal polarizer P₁ transmits half of the unpolarized intensity: I₁ = ½ I₀ = 64.0 W m⁻². Analyzer A then transmits I = I₁ cos²(25°) = ½(128) cos²(25°) = 52.6 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ½ I₀ cos²(25°) = 52.6 W m⁻² (B).

items.workedSolution: (a) E / E₀ = cos(50°) = 0.643. (b) I = I₀ cos²(50°) = 34.7 W m⁻². (c) Absorbed intensity = 84 − 34.7 = 49.3 W m⁻².

Subtracts transmitted intensity from incident intensity.

workingSteps: Apply Malus's law I = I₁ cos²θ.

parts.prompt: Determine the overall fraction I / I₀ of the original unpolarized intensity transmitted by the two-filter combination.
workingSteps: Overall transmission fraction = I / I₀ = ½ cos²θ.

items.stem: Figure shows unpolarized radiation of intensity 192 W m⁻² entering a liquid-crystal display (LCD) backlight test rig using thin-film linear polaroid sheets, traversing ideal vertical polarizer P₁ followed by linear analyzer A inclined at θ = 70° relative to P₁ (Malus's law for polarized light: I = I₁ cos²θ).
items.workedSolution: (a) After P₁, I₁ = ½ I₀ = 96.0 W m⁻². (b) After analyzer A, I = I₁ cos²(70°) = 11.2 W m⁻². (c) Overall fraction I / I₀ = ½ cos²(70°) = 0.0585.

Divides final transmitted intensity by incident unpolarized intensity I₀.

items.stem: Using a geotechnical seismic array, a snapshot of horizontally polarized surface waves in bedrock travelling to the right shows an amplitude of 0.042 m and a wavelength of 0.32 m. If the wave source oscillates at 55 Hz, what is the propagation speed of the wave?
items.workedSolution: From the displacement–position profile, wavelength λ = 0.32 m and frequency f = 55 Hz. Using the wave equation v = fλ = 55 Hz × 0.32 m = 17.6 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v = fλ to obtain 17.6 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides wavelength by frequency (λ / f), confusing frequency f with period T.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the wavelength by misreading a two-cycle span as a single wavelength.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides frequency by wavelength (f / λ) instead of applying v = fλ.

items.stem: Measurements from a high-speed motion tracker on a physics laboratory slinky-spring track show a sinusoidal wave of amplitude 0.024 m and wavelength 1.2 m travelling rightwards at a speed of 18 m s⁻¹. Which value gives the wave frequency?
items.workedSolution: Using f = v / λ with wave speed v = 18 m s⁻¹ and wavelength λ = 1.2 m gives f = 18 / 1.2 = 15.0 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Rearranges v = fλ to obtain f = v / λ = 15.0 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the oscillation period T = λ / v instead of the frequency f = v / λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Mistakes two full cycles for one wavelength, halving the calculated frequency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies wave speed by wavelength (vλ) instead of dividing v by λ.

items.stem: Figure shows a laser beam-expander test stage directing plane wavefronts onto a narrow vertical slit of aperture width 0.1 mm illuminated by coherent light of wavelength 650 nm, with a screen positioned 1.8 m behind the slit. Calculate the distance between the two first-order dark minima bounding the central maximum.
items.workedSolution: First diffraction minima lie at θ = ±λ / b, giving half-width y₁ = λD / b = 0.0117 m. Full central maximum width w = 2λD / b = 0.0234 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses w = 2λD / b to obtain 0.0234 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by slit width b and divides by screen distance D instead of 2λD / b.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates λD / b (the distance from the centre to one first-order minimum) instead of the full central maximum width 2λD / b.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by 4 instead of 2 when doubling the first-minimum half-width.

options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 4λD / w instead of 2λD / w.

items.stem: On a concert harp nylon string stretched between fixed tuning pins of length 0.72 m, transverse waves propagate at 90 m s⁻¹. What is the resonant frequency when the string vibrates in its n = 5 harmonic mode?
items.workedSolution: For a string fixed at both ends in harmonic n = 5, λ_n = 2L / n = 2(0.72) / 5 = 0.288 m. Thus f_n = v / λ_n = 90 / 0.288 = 313 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Applies f_n = nv / (2L) to obtain 313 Hz (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the closed-one-end pipe formula nv / (4L) instead of fixed-both-ends nv / (2L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in λ_n = 2L / n, computing f = nv / L.

items.stem: When a brass harpsichord wire stretched between fixed hitch and wrest pins of length 1.2 m vibrates in its n = 6 stationary-wave harmonic, a stroboscope measures its frequency as 480 Hz. Determine the wave speed along the wire.

markScheme.criterion: Computes λ_n = 2L / n and v = f_n λ_n = 192 m s⁻¹ (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = 4Lf_n / n to obtain 336 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses open-pipe wavelength 2L / n instead of closed-pipe 4L / n, halving the speed of sound.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes an even harmonic index (n − 1) instead of the odd harmonic n.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the n-th harmonic frequency as the fundamental mode v = 4Lf.

items.stem: Figure shows a cylindrical clarinet-model bore closed at the reed end and open at the bell (length 0.42 m, single open-end correction e = 0.022 m) resonating in odd harmonic n = 5 with sound speed 336 m s⁻¹. Calculate this resonant frequency.
items.workedSolution: Effective acoustic length for one closed and one open end is L_eff = L + e = 0.442 m. For odd harmonic n = 5, f_n = nv / (4L_eff) = (5 × 336) / (4 × 0.442) = 950 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds end correction 2e as if both ends were open, rather than L + e for a single open end.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the open-end antinode correction e, using physical length L instead of L + e.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses open-pipe denominator 2(L + e) instead of closed-pipe 4(L + e).

items.stem: Sound propagates at 336 m s⁻¹ in a cylindrical clarinet-model bore closed at the reed end and open at the bell of length 0.52 m (negligible end correction). Determine the resonant frequency when the air column vibrates in odd harmonic n = 3.
items.workedSolution: Effective acoustic length for one closed and one open end is L_eff = L + e = 0.520 m. For odd harmonic n = 3, f_n = nv / (4L_eff) = (3 × 336) / (4 × 0.520) = 485 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the n = 1 fundamental frequency v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the prohibited even harmonic (n − 1) into nv / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies open-both-ends formula nv / (2L) instead of closed-one-end nv / (4L).

items.stem: Figure depicts a narrow quartz acoustic resonator closed at one termination and open at the opposite end of length 0.85 m resonating in the lowest-frequency overtone above its fundamental mode. Taking the speed of sound as 348 m s⁻¹ and ignoring end correction, calculate this resonant frequency.
items.workedSolution: A pipe closed at one end supports odd harmonics only (n = 1, 3, 5, ...), so the next resonant mode above the fundamental is n = 3. Thus f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 3(348) / (4 × 0.85) = 307 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies odd harmonic n = 3 and computes f₃ = 3v / (4L) = 307 Hz (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the fundamental (first-harmonic) frequency v / (4L) instead of the first overtone 3v / (4L).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes an even n = 2 harmonic exists in a pipe closed at one end, computing 2f₁ = v / (2L) instead of 3f₁ = 3v / (4L).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the open-both-ends formula 3v / (2L) instead of closed-one-end 3v / (4L).
